# LYCHEE: Certified Screening of Inverted Lists for High-Recall Vector Search Dongfang Zhao
University of Washington, Tacoma School of Engineering and Technology
dzhao@uw.edu **Abstract** Nearest-neighbor search over embedding vectors now matches faces against watchlists, transactions against known fraud patterns, and medical images against confirmed cases, where a missed neighbor is a missed threat, fraud, or diagnosis. Because an approximate index cannot report which queries lost a true neighbor, these applications require recall of 0.999 to 0.9999, which cuts the misses of recall 0.99 by 10 to 100 times, at a cost far below that of exact search over billions of vectors. Conventionally, inverted-file indexes reach high recall by probing more lists. However, they read and score every probed vector at full precision, so that the throughput of a query falls in inverse proportion to the number of probed lists. On the other hand, graph indexes are fast at moderate recall but saturate below the high-recall targets, whereas quantized lists must rerank their candidates with the full vectors. Our insight is to decide for almost every probed vector that it cannot enter the top _k_ of the probed lists without reading the vector, through the certified lower bound of exact search by certified exclusion. This paper turns the above insight into LYCHEE, a GPU inverted-file search that screens the probed lists on tensor cores under a threshold from anchors of the same lists, and that computes exact distances only for the few vectors that survive the screening, in increasing order of their certified bounds. We prove that LYCHEE returns exactly the _k_ nearest vectors of the probed lists, which is the answer of an inverted-file search at full precision, while it reads a few hundred full vectors per query regardless of the number of probed lists. We evaluate LYCHEE on eleven datasets from one million to one billion vectors against ten GPU and CPU baselines on two GPU servers. At equal recall with 200 probed lists, LYCHEE is 9.7 to 117 times faster than IVF-Flat of cuVS on the nine datasets of up to 100 million vectors, and 65 times faster on Deep-100M at recall 0.9997 with 1,000 probed lists. LYCHEE also reaches recall levels that CAGRA and HNSW do not reach, and it outruns exact search by certified exclusion by 5 to 18 times on the datasets of more than ten million vectors. On four GPUs, LYCHEE searches one billion vectors at recall 0.9999 and is 44.5 times faster than IVF-Flat on BIGANN-1B. ### 1 Introduction Nearest-neighbor search over embeddings increasingly decides outcomes in which a missed neighbor has a direct impact on real-world applications. In security, face recognition [12, 50] searches a watchlist for the nearest face embedding, so that a missed neighbor allows a wanted person to pass the check. In health care, retrieval of medical images [39] supports a diagnosis with the confirmed cases nearest to the image of a patient, so that a missed case withholds evidence from the physician. In finance, fraud and anti-money-laundering screening matches transactions against known fraud patterns and sanctioned parties, where a missed match is both a loss and a compliance violation. Legal discovery [24], the deduplication of training data [1, 35], and retrieval-augmented generation [36] over dense passage retrieval [28, 33, 34] similarly need every relevant document, near-duplicate, or passage. These applications need recall far above the 0.9 to 0.95 at which approximate indexes are usually compared, because the errors of an approximate index are silent. An index at recall 0.99 loses about one true neighbor in a hundred without reporting which queries lost one, so that no operator can detect or repair the miss. A screening service that answers one million identification queries per day at recall 0.99 therefore misses about ten thousand true matches per day. Since the misses scale with one minus the recall, recall 0.9999 reduces them to about one hundred. Ranking quality follows the same trend: on MS MARCO [40], the mean reciprocal rank (MRR@10) of the retrieved passages rises from 0.3295 at recall 0.957 to 0.3373 at recall 0.997, against 0.3378 for the exact neighbors (Section 4.2). Exact search with CertEx [64] removes the misses, but its cost grows in proportion to the dataset, whereas the embedding datasets of these applications, such as DINOv2 [45], CLIP [47], and DataComp [17], hold millions to billions of vectors. These applications therefore need recall of 0.999 to 0.9999 at the cost of an approximate index, which lies at the expensive end of its recall and throughput trade-off. The inverted-file (IVF) index [32, 53], as used in Faiss [14, 31] and cuVS [42], is the standard partition index for this trade-off, which splits the dataset into lists by _k_-means. A query then scans the vectors of its _np_ nearest lists, whose recall grows with _np_ because the true neighbors of a query near a list boundary lie in neighboring lists. However, IVF- Flat reads and scores every probed vector at full precision. On ImageNet DINOv2 embeddings, the throughput of IVF- Flat in cuVS falls from 562,367 to 3,450 queries per second

<tbc>(QPS) as _n<sub>p</sub>_ grows from 1 to 200 of 1,024 lists (Figure 1a), while recall at 10 rises from 0.860 to 0.999. The other families of indexes respond to this cost in two ways. First, compressed lists (IVF-PQ [32], ScaNN [26], RaBitQ [18]) shrink the scanned bytes but must rerank their candidates with the full vectors to reach high recall. Second, graph indexes such as HNSW [38] and CAGRA [44] visit few vectors per query but saturate below the targets: CAGRA reaches recall 0.986 at its largest search width on DINOv2.

One observation is that the probed lists of a high-recall query hold far more vectors than its answer needs. For instance, at _n<sub>p</sub>_=200, a DINOv2 query probes about 280,000 vectors. Almost all of them lie far outside the radius of the 10th neighbor, so that the exact top 10 among them can be certified from the full distances of fewer than 200 vectors (Figure 1b). A full-precision scan nevertheless spends its memory traffic and arithmetic on the far vectors. The cost of high recall in an IVF index is therefore the cost of proving that far vectors are far.

Our insight is to certify the exclusion of far vectors inside the probed lists from low-dimensional projections, rather than reading and scoring their full vectors. While exact search by certified exclusion (CertEx) [64] proves that distant vectors cannot belong to the global nearest neighbors through hardware-certified lower bounds on short projection rows, an IVF search requires certifying non- membership within an irregular, query-dependent subset of lists. Proving exclusion inside the probed lists requires bounding the _k_-th distance local to these lists from their own anchors, which enables tensor cores to screen candidate rows at a fraction of full-precision memory traffic. Full- precision reads and exact distances are then needed only for the few survivors whose bounds can still enter the probed top _k_, breaking the linear dependence of high-recall IVF search on the number of probed vectors.

This paper turns the above insight into Lychee, a GPU IVF search with certified screening of the probed lists. Lychee takes its threshold from exact distances to anchors of the probed lists, which bound the _k_-th distance within the lists from above. A routed tensor-core pass screens all (query, list) pairs of a batch at once, grouping the queries that probe a list so that every list streams through the tensor cores once per batch. The survivors of all lists of a query<tbc>

<tbc>are then verified together in increasing order of their certified bounds, until no remaining survivor can enter the top _k_. We prove that this procedure returns exactly the _k_ nearest vectors of the probed lists, namely the answer of IVF-Flat on the same lists.

Lychee changes the cost of high recall in an IVF index from the number of probed vectors to the number of survivors of the certified screening. On DINOv2, Lychee serves 217,195 QPS at recall 0.999 (_n<sub>p</sub>_=200), 63 times the throughput of IVF-Flat and 53 times that of IVF-PQ with refinement at the same recall. The evaluation spans eleven datasets from one million to one billion vectors, ten baselines that cover the inverted-file, graph, and exhaustive families on GPUs and CPUs, and two GPU servers with five H100 GPUs in total.

In summary, this paper makes the following contributions:

• We propose a list-local certified threshold for inverted- file search, which bounds the _k_-th distance within the probed lists from the exact distances and thereby admits the certified screening of excluded vectors inside the lists.<tbc>

• We prove that certified screening followed by tie- aware ordered verification returns exactly the _k_ nearest vectors of the probed lists and derive a cost model in which the full-precision reads of a query follow its survivors rather than its probed vectors.<tbc>

• We implement Lychee on GPUs with a routed tensor- core pass that screens all (query, list) pairs of a batch at once and verifies the survivors of all probed lists of a query together.<tbc>

• We evaluate Lychee on eleven datasets from one million to one billion vectors against ten GPU and CPU baselines on two GPU servers and show that Lychee is 9.7 to 117 times faster than IVF-Flat at equal recall with 200 probed lists and up to 44.5 times faster on one billion vectors on four GPUs.

## 2 Related Work

### Partition and quantization indexes.

Inverted lists of a coarse quantizer [32, 53] are the basis of the IVF indexes in Faiss [14, 31], cuVS [42], and vector databases such as Milvus [57], Manu [27], AnalyticDB-V [61], and VBase [63]. The inverted multi-index [3], revisited inverted indices [6], and SPANN [9] improve the partition and the probe order, while product quantization [32], optimized product quantization [21], additive quantization [4], ScaNN [26], RaBitQ [18], its extended variant [19], and IVF-RaBitQ on GPUs [51] compress the scanned vectors and rerank with full vectors [30]. These methods change which vectors are probed or how many bytes an approximate distance reads, whereas Lychee keeps the probed set of IVF-Flat and certifies the exclusion of probed vectors, so that its answer equals the exact top _k_ of the probed lists.

#### Graph indexes.

Graph indexes such as NSG \[16\], HNSW \[38\], DiskANN \[54\], Starling \[59\], and their filtered variants \[22, 46\] visit few vectors per query through greedy search on a neighborhood graph built by methods such as NN-Descent \[13\]. On GPUs, SONG \[65\], GGNN \[23\], CAGRA \[44\], BANG \[55\], and PilotANN \[25\] parallelize the search. Surveys \[58\] and benchmarks \[2, 52\] show that graph searches reach high throughput at moderate recall but saturate as the search width grows. Lychee instead reaches the recall of the inverted lists at every _n<sub>p</sub>_, up to 0.9999 on DINOv2, with a cost that grows with the survivors of the screening.

#### Exact search and lower bounds.

Lower-bounding filters for exact search date back to the GEMINI framework \[15\], the VA-file \[60\], metric trees such as AESA \[56\], vp-trees \[62\], M-trees \[10\], and cover trees \[8\], and iDistance \[29\], which exclude candidates whose lower bound exceeds a current threshold. In high dimensions these bounds lose their power \[7, 60\], so that GPU exact search falls back to brute force \[20, 31\]. CertEx \[64\] restores the power of the lower bound in high dimensions through a principal-component lift with a rounding certificate for tensor cores. Lychee applies this bound inside the probed lists of an IVF index under a list-local threshold, which yields the answer of IVF-Flat on the same lists.

## 3 Methodology

### 3.1 Preliminaries and Background

#### Inverted-file search.

An inverted-file index \[32, 53\] partitions a dataset \(\mathcal{X}=\{\mathbf{x}_1,\dots,\mathbf{x}_N\}\subset\mathbb{R}^D\) into _P_ lists _L_<sub>1</sub>_,...,L<sub>P</sub>_ around centers **c**<sub>1</sub>_,...,_**c**_<sub>P</sub>_ from _k_-means, assigning every vector to its nearest center. A query **q** ranks the centers by distance and probes the _n<sub>p</sub>_ nearest ones. The probed lists form the candidate set _S_(**q**), from which IVF-Flat returns the _k_ vectors that lie nearest to **q** under the squared Euclidean distance. Recall therefore depends on the lists and on _n<sub>p</sub>_ alone, because the scan of _S_(**q**) is exact up to floating- point rounding. Multi-index structures \[3\], learned routing \[6\], and balanced partitions for disk-resident data \[9\] refine the choice of _S_(**q**), although each of them still reads the vectors of the chosen lists. The scan of the probed lists dominates the cost of a high-recall query. A query reads |_S_(**q**)|≈_n<sub>p</sub>N/P_ vectors of 4_D_ bytes each, so that its memory traffic grows linearly with _n<sub>p</sub>_. GPU implementations such as Faiss \[31\] and cuVS \[42\] therefore spend the time of a high-recall query on this traffic. Compressed lists reduce the bytes per vector through product quantization \[21, 32\], anisotropic quantization \[26\], or randomized binary codes \[18, 51\]. However, the compressed distances reorder the candidates, so that high recall requires a refinement step \[30\] that reads the full vectors of a multiple of _k_ candidates per query. The cost of a high-recall IVF query is therefore set by its full-precision reads, either of the whole probed set or of the refined candidates.

#### Certified exclusion.

Recently, certified exclusion (CertEx) \[64\] was proposed to replace most full-precision reads with a certified test. Consider an orthonormal matrix \(V\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times m}\) of the _m_ principal directions of the dataset and its mean \(\mu\). CertEx lifts every vector to

\(\ell(\mathbf{x})=\big[V^\top(\mathbf{x}-\mu);\|(I-VV^\top)(\mathbf{x}-\mu)\|\big]\in\mathbb{R}^{m+1},\) (1)

The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality on the residual components then gives \(\|\ell(\mathbf{q})-\ell(\mathbf{x})\|\le\|\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{x}\|\) for every pair. The lifted rows are stored in half precision together with four certificate coordinates that bound their rounding errors, so that one tensor-core product of a query row with a vector row yields a lower bound \(\beta(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{x})\le\|\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{x}\|^2\) that holds under every rounding of the product. A vector **x** survives the screening of a query only if \(\beta(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{x})\le U(\mathbf{q})\), where _U_(**q**) bounds the squared distance of the _k_-th nearest neighbor from above. CertEx sets _U_(**q**) from the exact distances of sampled anchors, since any _k_ distinct vectors bound the _k_-th distance, and verifies the survivors in increasing order of \(\beta\) until the next bound exceeds the _k_-th exact distance found. Every vector that the screening excludes costs 2(_m_+5) bytes instead of 4_D_, because only the survivors are read at full precision. CertEx applies this test to the whole dataset, so that its exact search still screens all _N_ rows per query. In contrast, an inverted-file query needs only the _k_ nearest vectors of its probed lists, which requires a threshold that bounds the _k_-th distance within these lists.

### 3.2 Lychee Overview

Lychee performs approximate nearest-neighbor search by returning the exact top-_k_ candidates of the probed lists, matching the full-precision candidate ranking of IVF-Flat. Given a query \(\mathbf{q}\in\mathbb{R}^D\) and probed set \(S(\mathbf{q})=L_{j_1}\cup\cdots\cup L_{j_{n_p}}\), the target answer _A<sub>k</sub>_(**q**) minimizes the sum of squared distances over any _k_-subset:

\(A_k(\mathbf{q})=argmin_{T\subseteq S(\mathbf{q}),|T|=k}\sum_{\mathbf{x}\in T}\|\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{x}\|^2,\) (2)

with ties broken by index. Evaluating Eq. (2) exactly attains the recall of the inverted lists at every _n<sub>p</sub>_, leaving query latency and throughput as the only quantities to improve.

The cost of Eq. (2) is dominated by full-precision reads. Define _r<sub>k</sub>_(**q**) as the _k_-th smallest squared distance from **q** to _S_(**q**). Every vector of _S_(**q**) farther than _r<sub>k</sub>_(**q**) is excluded from _A<sub>k</sub>_(**q**), although a full-precision scan learns this fact only after reading the vector. Lychee instead proves exclusion from the low-dimensional lifted row of the vector, under a threshold \(U(\mathbf{q})\ge r_k(\mathbf{q})\) that the probed lists themselves provide.

Figure 2 illustrates the resulting search pipeline of a query batch across its three algorithmic stages. In Stage 1, the search identifies _n<sub>p</sub>_ probed lists and gathers exact distances to their anchors (Definition 3.1) to establish a list-local threshold \(U(\mathbf{q})\ge r_k(\mathbf{q})\) (Figure 2, panel 1). In Stage 2, a routed tensor-core pass groups queries probing the same<tbc>

candidate list _L<sub>j</sub>_ into a query group _G<sub>j</sub>_, screening their half- precision lifted rows on tensor cores and filtering out candidates whose certified lower bound \(\beta(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{x})\) exceeds _U_(**q**) (Figure 2, panel 2). In Stage 3, the survivors of all probed lists are aggregated per query and verified at full precision in increasing order of their certified bounds, terminating verification as soon as the lower bound reaches the current _k_-th exact distance _h<sub>k</sub>_ (Figure 2, panel 3).

## 3.3 List-Local Certified Threshold

The screening threshold of LyCHEE is established from exact distances to a small set of representative vectors chosen from the probed lists, termed _anchors_ (Figure 2, panel 1).

**Definition 3.1** (List Anchors and Probed Anchor Set)**.** Consider an inverted list \(L_j=(\mathbf{x}_{j,1},\dots,\mathbf{x}_{j,|L_j|})\subset\mathbb{R}^D\). For a fixed stride \(s\in\mathbb{N}^+\), the _anchors_ of _L<sub>j</sub>_ are the designated subset of stored vectors at regular index intervals:

\(\Omega(L_j)=\big\{\mathbf{x}_{j,i\cdot s}\big|1\le i\le\lfloor|L_j|/s\rfloor\big\}\subset L_j,\) (3)

whose full-precision representations are preserved in device memory. For a query **q** probing lists \(S(\mathbf{q})=\bigcup_{j\in J(\mathbf{q})}L_j\), where _J_(**q**)=(_j_<sub>1</sub>_,...,j<sub>n<sub>p</sub></sub>_) ranks cluster centers by distance \(\|\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{c}_{j_1}\|\le\cdots\le\|\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{c}_{j_{n_p}}\|\), the _probed anchor set_ \(\mathcal{A}(\mathbf{q})\subseteq S(\mathbf{q})\) is the sequence of the first _b_ anchors gathered from \(\Omega(L_{j_1})\), \(\Omega(L_{j_2})\),_..._ in center order, where \(b\ge k\) denotes the anchor budget.

Given A(**q**), LyCHEE computes the exact squared distance \(\|\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{x}\|^2\) for each anchor \(\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{A}(\mathbf{q})\). The list-local certified threshold is then

\(U(\mathbf{q})=(1+\tau)d_{(k)}\big(\mathbf{q},\mathcal{A}(\mathbf{q})\big),\) (4)

where _d_<sub>(_k_)</sub> is the _k_-th smallest exact squared distance among the anchors A(**q**), and \(\tau\) is a small relative slack that covers the rounding of the screening threshold. If the probed lists hold fewer than _k_ anchors, _U_(**q**) falls back to a bound that every stored vector satisfies, computed from the norm of the query and the largest norm of the stored vectors. The query then scans its fewer than (_k+n<sub>p</sub>)s_ probed vectors exactly.

**Proposition 3.2.** _Under Definition 3.1, if_ \(|\mathcal{A}(\mathbf{q})|\ge k\)_, then_ \(U(\mathbf{q})\ge r_k(\mathbf{q})\).

_Proof._ By Definition 3.1, the anchors are \(|\mathcal{A}(\mathbf{q})|\ge k\) distinct vectors of _S_(**q**). The _k_ nearest of them form a subset of _S_(**q**) of size _k_ whose largest squared distance is _d_<sub>(_k_)</sub>. The _k_-th smallest squared distance over the superset _S_(**q**) cannot exceed the largest distance of any of its subsets of size _k_, so that \(r_k(\mathbf{q})\le d_{(k)}\le U(\mathbf{q})\). □

The threshold of Proposition 3.2 is local to the probed lists. A threshold from anchors of the whole dataset bounds the _k_-th distance in the dataset, which is smaller than _r<sub>k</sub>_(**q**) when the probed lists miss some true neighbors. A screening under such a threshold could therefore return fewer than _k_ vectors of _S_(**q**). The list-local threshold instead keeps every member of _A<sub>k</sub>_(**q**) under the screening at every _n<sub>p</sub>_. Moreover, the anchors of the nearest lists come first, so that the budget _b_ spends exact distances on the anchors that are most likely to lie near **q** and keeps _U_(**q**) close to _r<sub>k</sub>_(**q**).

## 3.4 Routed Tensor Screening

Given the list-local threshold _U_(**q**) of each query from Stage 1, Stage 2 screens candidate vectors within probed lists on GPU tensor cores. A naive per-query scan cannot map onto tensor cores efficiently: each query probes a different subset of _n<sub>p</sub>_ lists, while an individual inverted list of a few thousand vectors offers too little work for a single query to fill a tensor-core tile. LyCHEE therefore batches _B_ queries and groups the queries that probe list _L<sub>j</sub>_ into a query group _G<sub>j</sub>_. The queries in _G<sub>j</sub>_ and the candidate vectors in _L<sub>j</sub>_ then form dense matrix tiles of 128\(\times\)128 rows on tensor cores (Figure 2, panel 2). Every list therefore streams through cache and tensor cores once per batch, however many queries probe it. All lists share the global basis _V_ of CertEx, so that one lifted row of a query screens all its probed lists; Section 4.6 shows that this basis excludes all but a few hundred probed vectors.

An in-register predicate compares \(\beta(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{x})\) against the threshold _U_(**q**) of that query, retaining vector **x** only if \(\beta(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{x})\le U(\mathbf{q})\). The vectors of list _Lj_ satisfying this predicate form the list survivors, depicted as coral dots in Figure 2 (panel 2). Aggregating these survivors over all _np_ probed lists of query **q** produces the complete candidate survivor set: \(C\leftarrow\big\{\mathbf{x}\in S(\mathbf{q})\big|\beta(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{x})\le U(\mathbf{q})\big\},\) (5) which is forwarded to Stage 3. The following proposition establishes that certified screening prunes unpromising vectors with zero false dismissals. **Proposition 3.3** (Screening Soundness)**.** _Consider the exact top-k nearest neighbors_ \(A_k(\mathbf{q})\subseteq S(\mathbf{q})\) _of query_ **q** _in its probed lists (Eq._ (2)_). If the list-local threshold satisfies_ \(U(\mathbf{q})\ge r_k(\mathbf{q})\)_, then every true neighbor survives the certified screening:_ \(A_k(\mathbf{q})\subseteq C\). _Proof._ Consider any vector \(\mathbf{x}^*\in A_k(\mathbf{q})\). By definition of the _k_-th distance, \(\|\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{x}^*\|^2\le r_k(\mathbf{q})\). Because the certified lower bound is sound under finite-precision arithmetic, \(\beta(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{x}^*)\le\|\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{x}^*\|^2\). By transitivity and the validity of the threshold, \(\beta(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{x}^*)\le r_k(\mathbf{q})\le U(\mathbf{q})\). Vector **x**∗ therefore satisfies the screening predicate, so \(\mathbf{x}^*\in C\). ## 3.5 Ordered Bound Verification In Stage 3, Lychee verifies the survivors of the screening in increasing order of their certified lower bounds \(\beta(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{x})\), computing exact squared distances \(\|\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{x}\|^2\) at full precision. Algorithm 1 summarizes the search of a query across the three stages. Lines 5 to 10 execute the ordered verification over the survivor set _C_. Verification stops as soon as the next lower bound, raised to 0 since a squared distance is never negative, reaches the current _k_-th exact distance _hk_ (Figure 2, panel 3). Every remaining survivor in _C_ then has an exact distance at least as large, so that it can at best tie with the _k_-th neighbor already found. Stopping verification at equality is critical for datasets with duplicate vectors (such as DataComp), in which thousands of candidates share the _k_-th distance of a query and would otherwise all be verified. The certified bound satisfies \(\beta(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{x})\le\|\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{x}\|^2\le U\), so that **x** belongs to _C_. Since \(A_k(\mathbf{q})\subseteq C\subseteq S(\mathbf{q})\), the _k_ smallest distances over _C_ are those over _S_(**q**), namely the distances of _Ak_(**q**). \(\square\) ## 3.6 Cost Analysis Algorithm 1 runs in time _O_(|_S_(**q**)|(_m_+5)+_bD_+|_C_|log|_C_|+_V_(**q**)_D_) per query, where _V_(**q**) counts the survivors verified in Lines 6 to 10. The four terms account for the certified screening on tensor cores, the exact distances of the anchors, the sort of the survivors, and the verification at full precision, compared to _O_(|_S_(**q**)|_D_) for IVF-Flat. The extra space per query is _O(b_+|_C_|). The memory traffic of Lychee depends on the probed rows primarily through the short lifted rows (2(_m_+5) bytes each). Full-precision 4_D_-byte reads are restricted to the _b_ anchors and _V_(**q**) verified survivors. Against the 4_D|S_(**q**)| bytes read by IVF-Flat, the per-query traffic ratio approaches 2_D/(m_+5) as _np_ grows (e.g., \(3\times\) for DINOv2 at _m_=507). The routed pass of Section 3.4 divides this traffic further, because a probed list streams through the tensor cores once for its whole query group _Gj_, whereas IVF-Flat reads the list once for every query that probes it. The reuse across the batch therefore accounts for the speedup on 8- bit descriptors, whose lifted rows are longer than the vectors (256 against 128 bytes for SIFT at _m_=123). Device memory per vector is 2(_m_+5)+4_D_ bytes when full vectors reside on the GPU and 2(_m_+5)+4_D/s_ bytes when they reside in pinned host memory, since only the anchors stay on the GPU at full precision. Finally, while CertEx \[64\] screens all _N_ lifted rows of the dataset, Lychee screens only the probed set |_S_(**q**)|≈_npN/P_, scaling down the screening work by _np/P_ (e.g., 9.8% of the lists on SIFT1M and 3.1% on BIGANN-100M at recall 0.999).

## 4 Evaluation

### 4.1 Experimental Setup

#### Datasets.

The evaluation covers eleven datasets of text and image embeddings and local descriptors, from one million to one billion vectors and from 96 to 960 dimensions, which test the certified screening on wide and narrow vectors at every scale ( 1). ImageNet DINOv2 holds the DINOv2 ViT-B/14 embeddings \[45\] of the training images of ImageNet \[11, 49\], queried by its validation images. GIST1M holds the 960-dimensional GIST descriptors \[43\] of the ANN-Benchmarks suite \[2\]. DataComp holds the CLIP ViT-L/14 embeddings \[47\] of 12.79 million web images of DataComp \[17\], which contain large groups of duplicate images. SIFT1M and the BIGANN prefixes hold the SIFT descriptors \[37\] of the BIGANN dataset \[30\] as 8-bit integers, the Deep1B prefixes hold the 96-dimensional image descriptors of Deep1B \[5\], and MS MARCO holds the 768-dimensional embeddings of its 8.8 million passages \[40\] by msmarco-distilbert-cos-v5 \[48\], normalized so that Euclidean distance ranks as cosine similarity, with the 6,980 labeled development queries. Ground truth is the exact top 10, which an exhaustive float64 search provides for the Deep1B prefixes and corrects for three queries of the official Deep1B list.

#### Platforms.

The experiments run on two GPU servers with the same GPU model and software stack, namely CUDA 12.6 with driver 560.35, PyTorch 2.14, and cuVS 26.10. The first server has one NVIDIA H100 GPU \[41\] with 94 GB of memory, 48 cores of an Intel Xeon Platinum 8468 processor, and 240 GB of host memory. It runs Lychee, IVF-Flat, IVF-PQ, and CAGRA on ImageNet DINOv2, SIFT1M, BIGANN-10M, BIGANN-100M, and DataComp, together with the width and list studies on ImageNet DINOv2 and SIFT1M. The second server has four H100 GPUs of the same model, which NVLink connects pairwise, 192 cores of the same processor, and 960 GB of host memory. It runs every method on GIST1M, Deep-10M, and Deep- 100M, the remaining baselines on the other datasets, and the billion-scale experiments on all four GPUs; every single- GPU experiment uses one of its GPUs. Every search pro<tbc>

<tbc>cesses all queries of a dataset at once.

#### Metrics.

Recall at 10 is the fraction of the true 10 nearest neighbors in the returned list, averaged over the queries. On DataComp, whose duplicate images make the ids of tied neighbors interchangeable, a returned vector counts as a true neighbor if its distance is at most the 10th true distance, as in standard benchmarks with ties \[52\]. Throughput is the number of queries divided by the wall-clock time of the search, including the probe, the screening, and the verification, as the best of two or three runs after one warm-up run. The throughput of one configuration differs by up to 4% between the separately timed runs of different sections. Exactness is checked separately: on every dataset, at 1 to 128 probed lists, every answer of Lychee equals the float64 top 10 of its probed lists, with the same ids or the same distances under ties, for 1,000 queries per dataset of up to ten million vectors and 500 per larger dataset.

#### Baselines.

The evaluation compares Lychee against ten baselines that cover the inverted-file, graph, and exhaustive families on GPUs and CPUs ( 2). IVF-Flat of cuVS \[42\] scans the probed lists at full precision and computes the answer of Eq. (2) in float32 on its own _k_-means lists. IVF-PQ compresses the vectors to _D/_2 bytes of 8-bit codes, and IVF- SQ quantizes every coordinate to 8 bits; both refine their top 4_k_ candidates with the full vectors. IVF-RaBitQ \[18, 19, 51\] stores 7-bit extended RaBitQ codes and runs with and without the same refinement; it failed to build on DataComp. CAGRA \[44\] builds a graph of degree 64 and sweeps its search width from 16 to 512, on every dataset except DataComp, whose duplicate groups made the CAGRA build fail. The exhaustive search of cuVS computes all float32 distances. On the CPU, the IVF-Flat index of Faiss \[14\], the HNSW index of hnswlib \[38\] with 32 links per node and a construction width of 200, and ScaNN \[26\] with its anisotropic 4-bit quantization and exact reordering run on all 192 cores of the second server. Finally, CertEx \[64\] returns the exact top 10 over the whole dataset by certified exclusion on one GPU. The IVF indexes use the lists of  1 and sweep the number of probed lists from 1 to 500, or to 1,000 on the datasets of 100 million vectors, whereas HNSW sweeps its search width from 16 to 1,024.

### Implementation.

Lychee is a CUDA extension on the GPU implementation of CertEx, whose kernels encode the query rows with their certificates, run the routed tensor- core pass, and verify the survivors. The evaluated instantiation uses the lifted width _m_=507 on the 768- and 960- dimensional datasets, _m_=123 on the SIFT datasets, and _m_=91 on the Deep1B prefixes, an anchor stride of _s_=16, an anchor budget of _b_=1,024, a threshold slack of \(\tau=10^{-4}\), and batches of 8,192 queries. The verification computes the exact distances in float64 with one warp per query, in rounds of at least 32 survivors. Float64 arithmetic costs little in this step, because a query verifies only a few hundred vectors. On Deep-100M and DataComp, Lychee keeps the full vectors in pinned host memory.

## 4.2 Passage Retrieval and Ranking Quality

Figure 3 traces one MS MARCO dev query through Lychee at 500 probed lists. The probed lists hold 1,086,390 passages, of which the certified screening on tensor cores keeps 914. The ordered verification then reads the full vectors of only 32 survivors before it returns the relevant passage at Rank 1. IVF-PQ with refinement returns the same passage at Rank 1, whereas its throughput at this setting is 1,025 queries per second against 115,163 for Lychee. Over all 6,980 dev queries at 500 probed lists, the two indexes reach an MRR@10 of 0.3334 and 0.3337 (Figure 4), so that Lychee matches the ranking quality of refined quantized lists at 112 times the throughput of IVF-PQ.

Figure 4 plots recall at 10 and MRR@10 against throughput on MS MARCO. At 500 of 4,096 lists, recall at 10 reaches 0.979. Lychee answers 115,163 QPS at this operating point<tbc>

<tbc>compared to 704 for IVF-Flat (164\(\times\) faster), and 201,220 vs 1,713 QPS at 200 probed lists (117\(\times\)). Quantized indexes with full-precision refinement (IVF-PQ and IVF-SQ) lag by 70\(\times\) to 112\(\times\) (serving 1,025 and 1,650 QPS), because every query still scans the quantized codes of all its probed passages, although the refinement reads only 4_k_ full vectors.

The right panel of Figure 4 evaluates the ranking quality of the retrieved passages. The float32 brute-force search of cuVS yields an MRR@10 of 0.3377 against official labels, slightly below the exact 0.3378, because its float32 distances order a few near-tied passages differently. Lychee preserves 0.3334 at 500 lists and 0.3357 at 1,000 lists. CAGRA explores fewer vectors at lower recall (\(\le 0.95\)), but saturates at recall 0.990 with 29,364 QPS and an MRR@10 of 0.3352. Lychee matches 0.990 recall at 65,178 QPS with higher MRR@10 (0.3357), delivering 2.2\(\times\) the throughput of CAGRA and 185\(\times\) that of IVF-Flat (352 QPS). Beyond recall 0.99 where probed lists cover half the corpus, exact search becomes more efficient: Lychee serves 21,457 QPS at recall 0.997, whereas exact CertEx retrieves the complete ground- truth passages with full MRR@10 (0.3378) at 47,630 QPS.

## 4.5 Billion-Scale Search on Multiple GPUs

Figure 9 evaluates one billion vectors on the four GPUs of the second server, which tests whether the gain of Lychee holds at the scale of the largest public benchmarks [52]. Both methods split the dataset into four contiguous shards of 250 million vectors with 16,384 _k_-means lists each, one shard per GPU. A query probes the _n<sub>p</sub>_ nearest lists of every shard, every shard returns the exact top 10 of its probed lists, and the host merges the four answers by distance. Lychee keeps the full vectors of its shard in pinned host memory and only its lifted rows and anchors on its GPU, whereas IVF-Flat keeps its shard on the GPU.

On BIGANN-1B, Lychee answers 21,108 queries per second at recall 0.998 (_n<sub>p</sub>_=200), 16,615 at recall 0.9998 (_n<sub>p</sub>_=500), and 13,032 at recall 0.9999 (_n<sub>p</sub>_=1,000), against 1,455, 583, and 293 for IVF-Flat, which is 14.5\(\times\), 28.5\(\times\), and 44.5\(\times\) faster at equal recall. The build of Lychee takes 122 s against 398 s for IVF-Flat. On Deep1B, a float32 shard of 250 million vectors occupies 96 GB and exceeds the memory of an H100, so that IVF-Flat cannot build its index on the four GPUs. The lifted rows and anchors of Lychee occupy about 70 GB per GPU, and Lychee answers 59,466 queries per second at recall 0.998, 43,333 at recall 0.9996, and 32,082 at recall 0.9999 after a build of 270 s. Lychee therefore searches one billion float32 vectors on a single server at recall 0.9999, a configuration that the full-precision lists of IVF-Flat cannot hold.

Figure 10 counts the probed vectors, the survivors of the certified screening, and the verified vectors per query as _n<sub>p</sub>_ grows, which tests the cost model of Section 3.6. On ImageNet DINOv2, the probed vectors grow from 1,361 to 653,749 per query in proportion to _n<sub>p</sub>_, while the survivors grow from 602 to 2,905 and the verified vectors only from 131 to 152. On BIGANN-10M, the probed vectors grow to 1,206,157 per query, whereas the survivors stay below 330 and the verification ends after its first round of 32 vectors. The lists that a larger _n<sub>p</sub>_ adds lie far from the query, so that<tbc>

### 4.8 Parameter Sensitivity

Figure 12 evaluates the two parameters of LyCHE, the lifted width _m_ and the number of lists, which test how tight the certified bound must be and how the partition trades list size against fineness. The left panel plots the throughput at 200 probed lists against _m_. On ImageNet DINOv2, the throughput grows from 2,542 queries per second at _m_=127 to 11,015 at _m_=255 and 219,325 at _m_=507, because the verified vectors per query fall from 90,008 to 18,438 and 151. Deep-10M and SIFT1M follow the same trend up to 382,500 and 516,305 queries per second at their widest rows. GIST1M peaks at _m_=507 (130,112 QPS), where _m_=763 costs more than it saves. Wider rows pay off until the verified vectors approach the 32 of the first verification round.

The right panel plots recall against throughput for 256, 1,024, and 4,096 lists on ImageNet DINOv2 at the same shares of probed lists. With 20% of the lists probed, LyCHEe serves 199,023, 215,598, and 96,728 queries per second at recall 0.9982, 0.9990, and 0.9997. Fewer and larger lists fill more of each tensor-core tile, because more queries of a batch probe the same list, whereas more lists raise the recall at a given share. The default of 1,024 lists for a million vectors balances both effects, with throughput varying by \(<2.3\times\) across a 16-fold list range.

### 4.9 Ablation Study

3 isolates the two key components of LyCHEe, namely the list-local anchor threshold (Section 3.3) and the ordered bound verification (Algorithm 1). The global variant spreads the same budget of _b_=1,024 anchors evenly over the whole dataset, as CertEx does. Such a threshold does not guarantee \(U(\mathbf{q})\ge r_k(\mathbf{q})\) (Section 3.3), although its anchors lie mostly far from the query and make it much looser in practice than the _k_-th distance within the probed lists. Recall therefore stays at or above 0.999, whereas the survivors per query grow by 75.6\(\times\), 47.3\(\times\), and 256.8\(\times\) on ImageNet DINOv2, SIFT1M, and BIGANN-10M. The throughput drops accordingly by 18.8\(\times\), 2.0\(\times\), and 7.5\(\times\).

Without the ordered verification, every survivor is verified at full precision. The full-vector reads then grow by 16.0\(\times\), 6.5\(\times\), and 10.0\(\times\) on the same datasets, so that the throughput drops by 6.4\(\times\) (from 223,688 to 34,812 QPS on ImageNet DINOv2), 2.7\(\times\), and 3.4\(\times\). Both components are therefore necessary, since the threshold bounds the survivors, whereas the ordered verification bounds their full- precision reads.

## 5 Conclusion

High-recall search on inverted files spends its memory traffic on full-precision scans of the probed lists, while graph indexes saturate below the high-recall targets. LyCHEe bounds the _k_-th distance within the probed lists from their own anchors, screens the probed vectors on tensor cores with certified lower bounds, and verifies the few survivors in increasing order of their bounds, which returns exactly the answer of IVF-Flat on the same lists. On eleven datasets of up to one billion vectors and against ten GPU and CPU baselines, LyCHEe is up to 185\(\times\) faster than IVF-Flat at equal recall.
